lesson.title: Same Substance, New Form: Physical Changes
lesson.summary: This section defines physical change as an alteration in physical properties without a change in chemical identity, using melting and dissolving as key examples.
lesson.body:
The last two sections introduced physical and chemical properties as two different ways of describing a substance. Changes in matter can be sorted the same way, and a physical change is any transformation that alters one or more physical properties of a substance, such as its shape, size, or state, while leaving its chemical identity completely intact. Melting, freezing, boiling, condensing, dissolving, and simply breaking or crushing something into smaller pieces are all physical changes. When ice melts into liquid water, its density, hardness, and shape all change dramatically, but the substance is still made of the same H2O molecules before and after; no bonds within the water molecules themselves are broken, only the weaker attractions holding neighboring molecules in the rigid ice structure. Because no new substance forms, physical changes are usually reversible: liquid water refrozen becomes ice again, indistinguishable from the ice you started with.

Dissolving is a physical change that sometimes confuses students because it looks dramatic, a solid sugar cube seeming to vanish into a glass of tea, but nothing chemical has actually happened. When sucrose dissolves in water, the sugar molecules separate from each other and spread out among the water molecules, yet each sucrose molecule remains chemically unchanged, still C12H22O11, with all of its original atoms bonded exactly as before. You can confirm this is a physical change, not a chemical one, by evaporating the water away: the sugar reappears, chemically identical to what you started with, which is exactly the separation technique described in the mixtures section. If dissolving had been a chemical change, evaporating the water would leave behind a different substance entirely, not the original sugar.

Every physical change obeys conservation of mass: the total mass of matter present before the change equals the total mass present after, since no atoms are created, destroyed, or converted into a different element. If you carefully weigh 100 grams of ice, let it melt completely into liquid water without spilling any, and weigh the water, the scale still reads 100 grams. This might seem too obvious to mention, but it becomes an important checkpoint once chemical changes are introduced in the next section, where the same principle of conserved mass holds true even though the substances themselves are transformed into entirely new products, which is far less intuitive.

Physical changes are not always as reversible as melting and freezing suggest, and the ease of reversal is not actually what defines a change as physical; the test is always whether the chemical identity of the substance stays the same. Shattering a glass window is a physical change, and a very difficult one to reverse, but the glass, in whatever broken shape, is still chemically the same silicate material it was before it shattered, with the same chemical formula and the same chemical properties. Similarly, cutting a sheet of paper into a thousand tiny pieces is a physical change, however impractical it would be to reassemble. Keeping this distinction clear, chemical identity rather than reversibility, prepares you directly for the next section, where chemical changes are defined by the appearance of one or more genuinely new substances with new chemical properties.
